explanation: The molecular layer contains outer stellate cells, inner basket cells, Purkinje cell dendrites, Golgi cell dendrites, and parallel fibers (Granular cell axons); mossy fibers are in the granular layer.
Purkinje cells are the primary integrative neurons of the cerebellar cortex, receiving input from climbing and parallel fibers and outputting via their axons to deep nuclei.
Purkinje cells are large pyriform (pear-shaped) multipolar neurons with a characteristic flask-shaped cell body and extensive dendritic tree.
Golgi cells have large cell bodies with many long dendrites that extend into all cortical layers (not just the Golgi layer), and their axons synapse with granular cells in the granular layer.
Granular cells have T-shaped axons (parallel fibers) that run tangentially in the molecular layer, forming excitatory synapses with Purkinje cell dendrites.
Purkinje cells are excited by climbing fibers, mossy fibers (indirectly via granule cells), and parallel fibers; basket and Golgi cells provide inhibitory input.
The cerebral medulla contains afferent/efferent fibers, dentate nuclei, and Purkinje fiber axons; Purkinje cells themselves are in the cerebellar cortex, not the medulla.
The medial longitudinal fasciculus continues in the spinal cord via the vestibulospinal and sulcomarginal tracts, coordinating head-eye movements.
Border cells (meningothelial cells) between arachnoid and dura are attached by both tight junctions and desmosomes for structural integrity.
Leptomeninges refers to the pia mater and arachnoid mater together, which are delicate membranes lying between the dura mater and subarachnoid space.
The pia mater consists of a single layer of modified fibroblasts (mesothelial cells) that closely follow the contours of the brain and spinal cord.
The arachnoid barrier cell layer is present between extracerebral capillaries and the subarachnoid space, regulating CSF composition.
The blood-brain barrier consists of thick basement membrane, non-fenestrated endothelium, and astrocyte foot processes; ependymal cells form the CSF barrier, not BBB.
Tight junctions (zonulae occludentes) between endothelial cells and ependymal cells create the selective permeability barrier in the CNS.
The blood-CSF barrier is formed by endothelial cells, basement membrane, and ependymal cells with tight junctions; astrocyte foot processes are part of the BBB, not blood-CSF barrier.
The blood-brain barrier consists of endothelial cells, basement membrane, and astrocyte foot processes; ependymal cells with tight junctions form the ventricular lining, not the BBB.
The CNS lacks connective tissue (except at surfaces), making it soft; this also explains its vulnerability to mechanical injury.
Grey matter is central in spinal cord with neuron cell bodies; white matter is peripheral with myelinated fibers; the CNS lacks connective tissue framework.
Grey matter contains neuron cell bodies and unmyelinated fibers; white matter contains myelinated fibers; the distribution depends on myelin location.
The central canal is lined by simple cuboidal epithelium (ependymal cells) that is partially ciliated, similar to the ventricular lining.
Grey matter contains nerve cell bodies, neuroglial cells, and unmyelinated fibers; myelinated nerve fibers are found in white matter.
Lumbar level has the smallest white matter/grey matter ratio because it has relatively less white matter (fewer descending motor fibers passing through).
Thoracic spinal cord has lateral horns (intermediolateral cell columns) containing sympathetic preganglionic neurons, giving it 4 horns.
Cervical spinal cord has the largest white matter/grey matter ratio because it contains the most descending and ascending fibers passing to/from the brain.
Dorsal spinocerebellar tract carries proprioceptive information to the cerebellum (subcortical level); other tracts listed go to thalamus/cortex.
Proprioception receptors include muscle spindles, Golgi tendon organs, and joint receptors (Pacinian corpuscles at joints), providing limb position sense.
Pacinian corpuscles are rapidly adapting deep pressure and vibration receptors with a characteristic lamellar structure in the dermis.
First order neurons in proprioception from the lower body have cell bodies in the dorsal root ganglia (spinal ganglia) at corresponding levels.
First order neurons in proprioception from the upper body also have cell bodies in dorsal root ganglia (spinal ganglia), same as lower body.
Second order neurons for lower body proprioception are in the gracile nucleus on the same side, which then decussates as internal arcuate fibers.
Internal arcuate fibers (second order proprioceptive neurons crossing) are present in the closed medulla where the gracile and cuneate nuclei are located.
External arcuate fibers carry proprioceptive and vestibular information to the cerebellum via the peduncles, forming the mossy fiber input.
The gracile tract carries proprioception from the lower half of the body (sacral, lumbar, lower thoracic) and terminates in the gracile nucleus of the medulla.
The cuneate tract arises from spinal ganglia in the upper half of the body (cervical and upper thoracic) and carries upper limb proprioception.
Anterior external arcuate fibers connect the gracile and cuneate nuclei of the same side to the cerebellum via the inferior cerebellar peduncle.
